Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction — Rigid contacts: from point velocity to a persistent contact manifold Scope: original, independently reconstructed teaching for the existing engine collision-response narrative. The executable witnesses are rigid_contact_lab.cpp and persistent_contact_lab.cpp. These are 2D velocity-level CPU witnesses; they do not claim to be Kairo’s engine implementation, 3D production manifold generation, or continuous collision detection. Symbols and sign conventions below follow those two witnesses. Why a contact is a constraint rather than a force chosen by eye Imagine a box descending onto a static floor. The collision detector reports that the geometry is touching or overlapping, but it does not say which velocities are physically admissible. With body A as the floor and body B as the box, define the contact normal n to point from A toward B. At contact position p, the lever arms measured from each body’s centre of mass are r_A = p − x_A and r_B = p − x_B. For a planar rigid body, its point velocity is v(p) = v_com + ω × r, where planar scalar angular speed ω produces ω × (r_x,r_y) = (−ω r_y, ω r_x). This matters because an object rotating toward the floor can be closing at a corner even when the centre of mass is moving away. The relative velocity of the two material points is u = (v_B + ω_B × r_B) − (v_A + ω_A × r_A). The normal component u_n = u · n tells us whether those two points are closing (u_n < 0) or separating (u_n > 0). For a non-penetrating unilateral contact without restitution, the desired post-solve condition is u_n ≥ 0, with a nonnegative accumulated contact impulse λ_n ≥ 0. Their complementarity condition is λ_n u_n = 0 at an exact solution: either the contact carries a positive separating-prevention impulse and reaches zero normal speed, or the bodies separate freely and the contact carries no impulse. Finite-iteration solvers only approximate this coupled condition. Deriving effective inverse mass, rather than memorizing its denominator The impulse on B is +λ n and the reaction on A is −λ n. Newton’s linear momentum law gives Δv_B = +λ m_B⁻¹ n and Δv_A = −λ m_A⁻¹ n. Angular impulse about the centre of mass gives Δω_B = +λ I_B⁻¹ (r_B × n) and Δω_A = −λ I_A⁻¹ (r_A × n), where the planar cross product of vectors is the scalar r_x n_y − r_y n_x. A rotation changes point velocity through Δω × r, and its projection onto n adds an angular term proportional to the squared lever arm. Consequently the normal relative velocity changes by Δu_n = k_n λ, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>m</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>m</mi> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>I</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>I</mi> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math> Here k_n is inverse effective mass in the contact direction, not mass itself. The same physical impulse changes normal speed less when the effective mass is large. The equation follows from the full point-velocity update; it is not valid to omit rotational terms whenever the contact is off-centre. A static body uses zero inverse mass and inertia, but two completely unresponsive bodies yield k_n = 0 and must not be divided by. The corresponding tangential value k_t is obtained by substituting the perpendicular unit tangent t = (−n_y, n_x) for n. For a desired post-impact normal speed b, one unconstrained correction is Δλ = (b − u_n)/k_n. A real contact cannot pull the bodies together, so the accumulated normal multiplier is projected: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msubsup> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>w</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>o</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>u</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </math> Apply only the difference, Δλ_n = λ_n^{new} − λ_n^{old}, to body velocities. Applying the whole accumulated value every iteration would add the same historical impulse repeatedly, making motion energy grow artificially. Conversely, resetting the accumulator on every sweep defeats the projected Gauss–Seidel interpretation and prevents reliable friction bounds. Restitution is a contact-creation decision, not a new bounce each iteration For an impact with pre-solve normal speed u_n^before < −v_threshold, the outgoing speed target in this simplified solver is b = −e u_n^before, with restitution coefficient e ∈ [0,1]. This target must be sampled before contact impulses change the velocity and then held fixed during the iteration. If a solver recomputes b from the current velocity at every visit, a persistent resting point can acquire artificial new bounce energy. The witness distinguishes a new impact from a persistent contact through an explicit newImpact argument; a production engine requires an actual contact-state machine and impact detection so the decision is not left to a careless caller. For the central collision test, both bodies have mass 1 kg, A starts at 2 m/s, B at 0 m/s, and the normal is +x. Their relative closing speed is −2 m/s; with e=1 and k_n=2 kg⁻¹, we need Δλ_n = (2 − (−2))/2 = 2 kg·m/s. The resulting velocities are 0 m/s and 2 m/s. Linear momentum remains 2 kg·m/s, and the kinetic energy remains 2 joules. This equality is specific to the elastic, frictionless, central, idealized two-body case—not a conservation promise for frictional or inelastic impacts. Why friction depends on the normal impulse For the upward normal n=(0,1) the laboratory chooses the tangent t=(−1,0). The sliding box initially moves at +3 m/s in x, so its tangent-coordinate velocity is u_t = −3 m/s. The unconstrained tangent impulse is −u_t/k_t; here k_t=1 kg⁻¹, giving +3 kg·m/s. The normal collision supplies λ_n=2 kg·m/s. With coefficient μ=0.5, the Coulomb limit is μλ_n=1 kg·m/s, so the stored tangent impulse is +1, not −1. Multiplying +1 × (−1,0) produces an x-directed impulse of (−1,0), reducing the box’s x velocity from +3 to +2 m/s. The sign of the stored scalar is relative to the chosen tangent direction; it cannot be interpreted without that basis. The projected update is λ_t^{new} = clamp(λ_t^{old} − u_t/k_t, −μλ_n, +μλ_n). This is a scalar tangent model for 2D; real 3D contact has a two-dimensional tangent plane and requires a disk-cone constraint or a chosen approximation. The witness applies a single coefficient and does not model static-versus-dynamic friction transition, anisotropy, rolling friction, torsional friction or compliant materials. Why a manifold needs persistent identity and sequential sweeps A wide box can contact a floor at two corners. Both rows modify the same centre-of-mass velocity and angular velocity. Solving one row therefore changes the velocity seen by the next row. A one-pass independent pair of impulses is not equivalent to solving their coupled system. The reference witness stores two world-space contact points, evaluates each row in sequence, and repeats sweeps. The residual normal speeds and angular velocity are checked after twenty sweeps. Its iteration result is deterministic for its fixed row order but should not be advertised as an order-independent exact solution. On the next frame, a geometry matcher must identify whether each physical contact feature persisted. If the same feature, body pair, contact orientation, and compatible basis survive, previously accumulated impulses are useful initial guesses. Warm-start once by applying the cached impulses to the newly constructed pre-solve velocities before iteration. Never warm-start twice, and never reuse a tangential scalar after rotating the tangent basis without transforming it. A changed feature ID, reversed A/B order, altered normal, teleport, or discontinuous mass/inertia change may invalidate the cache. The witness includes a feature ID as data but does not implement feature matching; that is a separate production requirement. Caches may also require dt-aware scaling when timestep changes, and a true contact solver must decide how speculative contacts and missed or sleeping frames are handled. Warm-starting can improve convergence, but it is not a substitute for manifold quality. Contact identity: why matching by memory address or contact index is insufficient The physical reaction at a point can be reused between frames only if the cache still refers to the same interacting surface features. When two faces touch, clipping may produce two manifold points whose array order changes as the bodies rotate. If we cache impulse #0 against array position #0, a later reordering can accidentally apply the left-corner impulse at the right corner, creating a torque that was never physically demanded. A robust narrow phase should assign each contact a stable feature pair, for example an incident vertex/edge identifier and reference face identifier, with deterministic canonicalization of body ordering. These identifiers are geometric facts maintained by collision generation, not sequential indices assigned by a container. The executable contact-cache witness concentrates on the subsequent policy rather than inventing a complete polygon clipper. The Key holds canonical body IDs plus two feature identifiers. The map stores the previously accepted normal and tangent impulse, its local normal direction, the previous friction coefficient, timestep, and last-seen frame. The cache is valid only if the same key was seen on the immediately preceding frame, the normal has changed by no more than 15 degrees, and the new timestep is between half and twice the cached timestep. These are documented laboratory thresholds, not universally optimal thresholds or engine-wide facts. The code rejects reversed body order because reversing A and B changes the sign of the normal and impulse convention. A tangent impulse is a vector in world space, although this 2D solver stores it as one scalar relative to a perpendicular tangent. When the normal rotates from n_old to n_new, the tangent axes t_old=(-n_old.y,n_old.x) and t_new=(-n_new.y,n_new.x) also rotate. The old physical friction impulse is P_t_old=λ_t_old t_old. The scalar along the new tangent is its dot projection: $ \lambda{t,new}^{seed} = \frac{\Delta t_{new}}{\Delta t_{old}} \left(\lambda{t,old},\mathbf t_{old}\cdot\mathbf t_{new}\right). $ The normal cache receives the same heuristic timestep ratio, and the tangent is clamped to ± μ_new λ_n_new. With an old upward normal (0,1), the old tangent is (-1,0). If the normal turns 10 degrees, the tangent projection of a previous scalar impulse 0.5 is 0.5 cos(10°) ≈ 0.492404, while the world impulse direction has changed consistently. Reusing 0.5 unchanged would preserve the scalar but not the intended projection onto the new contact tangent. This linear projection is a warm-start heuristic, not an exact solution of the new contact constraint; the subsequent iterative solver must still correct its residual. An edit to the friction coefficient clears only the tangential cached impulse in this experiment, retaining the normal impulse if all other validity rules pass. A material change in restitution, velocity discontinuity, teleport, substantial mass/inertia change, sleeping transition, or topology discontinuity may also require cache rejection in a production system and is not automatically detected by this small input type. Impulse scaling by timestep ratio is similarly a common starting heuristic, not an unconditional physical identity; the test exercises ratios 0.5, 1, and 4 and rejects the last. A caller must invoke begin_frame, use lookup to seed each new manifold row, warm-start those rows once, run velocity iterations, store each final impulse exactly once, and prune stale entries. Pruning at the wrong moment can erase still-needed contacts; storing duplicate feature keys silently makes iteration results depend on array ordering, so the witness rejects duplicates. The implementation has a testable boundary: it assumes a reliable feature matcher has already produced identifiers, that contact validity has been established by the geometry system, and that stable body IDs are never prematurely recycled. A generation-counted body handle would be safer than an integer object index alone. The cache does not detect 3D tangent-frame rotation, it does not calculate a physically accurate contact point, and its ordered map is a reference implementation rather than a measured real-time allocation strategy. A production engine should benchmark a preallocated flat hash map or per-pair cache with explicit frame ownership and deterministic iteration requirements. Velocity correction is not penetration correction The equations above change velocities. They do not, by themselves, repair existing overlaps in positions. A production pipeline generally needs a distinct and carefully scoped policy: geometry generation and signed separation, speculative contact margins, split impulses or position-level stabilization, and consistent timestep handling. Naively adding a large position-error velocity bias can inject energy, make stacks jitter, or break restitution. This CPU witness intentionally has no position integrator, no Baumgarte term, no split impulse and no continuous collision detection. Therefore its passing tests cannot establish the correctness of CCD tunneling prevention or deep-overlap recovery. From end-of-frame overlap to continuous time of impact The contact solver described above only acts on contacts it has been given. A fast-moving disk can start to the left of a thin obstacle and finish to the right of it without overlapping at the end of a fixed simulation step. If collision detection samples positions only at the step boundary, it sees no collision, so even a mathematically perfect impulse solver cannot prevent tunneling. This is the reason continuous collision detection (CCD) is a separate geometric question: what is the first time, within the proposed integration interval, when the moving shapes touch? For two disks with initial centres x_A and x_B, constant velocities v_A and v_B, and radii r_A, r_B, define the relative centre separation p = x_B - x_A, relative velocity v = v_B - v_A, and sum of radii R = r_A + r_B. Their separation at time t is p(t) = p + tv. They first touch when the squared centre distance equals the squared radius sum: $ \lVert \mathbf p+t\mathbf v\rVert2=R2. $ Expanding the dot product gives the quadratic $ at^2+bt+c=0,\qquad a=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v,\quad b=2\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf v,\quad c=\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p-R^2. $ The meaning of the coefficients is crucial. c is the initial squared-distance gap: c<0 means the disks are already overlapping and this witness returns t=0, assigning overlap correction to a separate solver; c=0 means initial touching. If a=0, the relative geometry never moves during the interval. For initially separated disks, b≥0 means squared distance is not initially decreasing, so a collision cannot occur under these constant velocities. A discriminant D=b²−4ac<0 means the motion line misses the expanded-radius disk. D=0 gives a tangent or grazing touch, which counts as a contact in this laboratory. The familiar quadratic expression (-b−sqrt(D))/(2a) can lose precision when nearly equal quantities are subtracted. The swept-disk CPU witness instead computes a stable intermediate q = -0.5(b − sqrt(D)) in its restricted b<0 branch, then evaluates the roots as t_near = c/q and t_far = q/a. Their product remains c/a, and the smaller root is tested against 0≤t≤Δt. The code uses std::fma in the discriminant to avoid one rounding step, but this is still finite-precision arithmetic; reliable collision detection across extreme dynamic ranges needs scale-aware error analysis or a more robust predicate policy. Consider a disk of radius 1 m stationary at the origin and another radius-1 disk initially at x=10 m moving left at 100 m/s. Its centre must move 8 m before touching, so the time of impact is 0.08 s. At Δt=0.1 s, the moving disk would end at the origin and overlap if sampled; for an even faster moving disk it could end past the obstacle and be missed entirely. An analytical time-of-impact query reports the 0.08 s encounter regardless of the end position. During a simulation step, a practical engine can advance up to this impact, generate a contact normal, solve or schedule the event, and then advance the remaining time, with a bounded substep count and an explicit policy for simultaneous events and resting contacts. The event’s collision normal is the normalized relative separation n(t) = (p+tv)/|p+tv|, pointing A to B. When initial centres coincide, there is no unique geometric normal; the witness uses a deterministic velocity-based fallback or +x if relative velocity is zero. This fallback is a test policy rather than a geometrically determined surface normal. The tests explicitly examine grazing touch, no-hit trajectories, hits outside the requested frame, existing overlap, coincident centres, invalid parameters, a high-dynamic-range trajectory, and Galilean invariance under equal velocity added to both bodies. The latter should not change relative motion or time of impact. What this does not solve: disk CCD assumes translational linear motion throughout the interval and fixed radii. It does not include forces or acceleration changing the trajectory, rotation of polygons, concave meshes, vertex-edge events, general convex support functions, conservative advancement, broadphase swept bounds, contact island rescheduling, stable substep integration, or CCD after multiple impulses. It also does not prove the absence of false misses at all floating-point scales. These exclusions must be explicit when moving from a CPU analytic oracle to the engine’s full collision pipeline. A complete impact event: geometry, first time, impulse and remaining interval The earlier swept-disk query identifies an impact but does not evolve a scene. The independent disk event pipeline laboratory connects geometry, state integration, simultaneous constraints and the remainder of the frame. It does not claim to be Kairo’s actual world step. The model assumes fixed-radius, non-spinning disks, piecewise constant velocities, instantaneous frictionless impulses, and linear motion between impacts. There are no forces, torque, resting-contact stabilization, soft contacts or arbitrary polygons. The entire algorithm follows from keeping one variable: remaining time. At each iteration, query all unordered disk pairs for their first collision in that remaining interval. If no pair collides, advance every position by its current velocity times the entire remaining interval. If collisions exist, find the earliest time, move all disks to that instant, collect other impacts at approximately the same time, freeze each event’s incoming normal velocity and restitution target, solve their normal impulses, then repeat the time-of-impact scan because the impulses have changed the future motion. The numerical trace is visible in the first laboratory test. A radius-1 stationary disk is at x=0. Another radius-1 disk starts at x=10 with velocity −100 m/s, and the requested frame duration is 0.10 s. The moving disk must travel 8 m before the two surfaces meet, giving TOI=0.08 s. The world advances both disks through 0.08 s, then an elastic impulse against the infinite-mass disk reverses its incoming velocity to +100 m/s. The remaining time is 0.02 s, so its centre ends at x=4 m. An end-of-frame overlap test cannot reconstruct this physically meaningful trajectory by merely reversing the velocity at t=0.10 s. For non-spinning disk collisions along the line of centres, the inverse effective mass is the sum of inverse masses, k = m_A⁻¹ + m_B⁻¹. With unit collision normal n pointing from A to B, relative normal speed u_n=(v_B−v_A)·n, and fixed impact target b=−e u_n_before, the solver’s unilateral accumulated impulse is $ \lambda{next}=\max\left(0,\lambda{previous} +\frac{b-(\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_A)\cdot\mathbf n} {m_A{-1}+m_B{-1}}\right). $ Only the difference Δλ = λ_next − λ_previous changes velocities. In a simultaneous batch, multiple contact rows may share a disk, so each row modifies the velocities seen by subsequent rows. The laboratory runs 32 sequential sweeps, freezing the original bounce target rather than repeatedly inventing a new restitution event. A symmetric three-disk scene tests two simultaneous impacts; another three-disk scene tests two impacts at different times in one frame. The discovery procedure is O(n²) for each rescan because it checks every unordered pair, with no spatial acceleration. The same-time grouping threshold and near-touch geometry threshold are explicit finite-precision policies, not robust computational-geometry predicates. Grazing trajectories with zero closing normal speed are skipped. Deep initial overlaps are rejected rather than repaired. An event budget throws when exhausted, preventing an infinite event loop from masquerading as successful advancement. Importantly, a thrown exception can leave the input scene partly advanced: a production caller needs a rollback snapshot or transactional step if partial state mutation is unacceptable. The nine deterministic tests exercise fast impacts, isolated elastic momentum and energy conservation, simultaneous row coupling, separating pairs, initial overlap rejection, event-budget exhaustion, chained events, ideal inelastic energy loss, and zero-duration/duplicate-ID validation. These tests establish a small analytic oracle, not a general proof of energy or convergence for arbitrary many-body simultaneous collisions, a guarantee against floating-point tunneling, support for rotating convex objects, or a persistent resting-contact engine. For an impact against an externally fixed body, momentum conservation of the two displayed disks alone is not the correct closed-system invariant; the stationary environment receives the reaction. Reducing collision search without losing collisions: conservative swept bounds The event-step laboratory above asks every pair of disks whether they will collide during the remaining time interval. With n bodies, this examines n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs after each event. For 1,000 disks, that is 499,500 expensive exact pair-time queries per scan—even if almost every disk is far away from the others. A broad phase exists to reject pairs that cannot possibly interact using a cheaper geometric test; it is not allowed to reject a true collision merely to be fast. This is why the central proof obligation is conservative coverage, not an attractive benchmark on one scene. For a disk of radius r, initial centre p=(p_x,p_y), velocity v=(v_x,v_y) and remaining interval Δt, its centre under constant velocity travels along the segment from p to p+vΔt. Every possible disk position lies inside its swept axis-aligned rectangle. Its x bounds are min(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)−r and max(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)+r; y is analogous. The swept-broadphase reference lab conservatively rounds each boundary one representable floating-point value outward with std::nextafter. The exact continuous disk shape is a capsule around the segment, while its swept AABB is a larger rectangle: the rectangle admits extra pairs but must not discard any collision, provided the endpoints and bounds are correctly represented. The algorithm sorts these rectangles by their minimum x coordinate, breaking ties by stable disk ID. As it visits each new rectangle, it removes from an active set any earlier rectangle whose maximum x lies strictly before the current minimum x. Every remaining active rectangle overlaps along x; the algorithm then compares their y intervals. Pairs that pass both checks are returned in deterministic lexicographically sorted index order, with a duplicate assertion. A true disk impact at time t∈[0,Δt] means the two disk regions intersect at that time; their swept AABBs must both contain the intersection point. Therefore their AABBs overlap in x and y and the pair must survive the broad-phase filtering. The reverse implication is false: AABBs may overlap even when the disks pass at different times or miss geometrically. The exact TOI narrow phase must therefore test every candidate before scheduling an event. The laboratory compares its candidate set with an independent analytic disk TOI predicate, rather than comparing the broad phase against itself. Each true TOI pair must appear in the returned set. It tests a high-speed crossing, 100 stationary well-spaced disks with zero candidates, 200 seeded randomized scenes containing 35 disks each, and malformed identity/time inputs. The random scenes therefore examine up to 119,000 unordered pairs for conservative coverage, because each 35-disk scene contains 595 pairs. These are useful regression witnesses, not a proof against all finite-precision failures. Sorting has O(n log n) comparison cost. Maintaining the simple active vector has potentially O(n²) scanning and removal cost when many broad AABBs overlap; the output itself can contain O(n²) candidate pairs in a dense scene. A scalable production version may use a better interval structure, broadphase BVH, grid, or incremental pair cache, and should benchmark temporally coherent motion rather than assuming this sample has production throughput. The original broadphase witness remains independently testable; the event stepper now has an optional swept-candidate mode alongside its exhaustive reference mode. Both generate candidate pairs for the current remaining interval, and the event stepper rebuilds candidates after each velocity-changing impact. A differential test source is committed to compare complete outcomes, but its successful GitHub-hosted execution remains unverified. This code-level integration is not yet native Kairo runtime integration or evidence of speedup. How to reconstruct and verify the witness Read the Row fields as a prepared contact Jacobian in compressed form: ra/rb are the lever arms, n/t are the constraint axes, kn/kt are scalar rows of the matrix J M⁻¹ Jᵀ. The method relative_velocity computes Jv, inverse_effective_mass computes a row’s inverse effective mass, solve_one projects impulse increments, and warm_start applies an already-owned cache once. make_row validates data and freezes the impact target. The six tests cover central momentum/energy, friction orientation, angular impulse, separating and static degeneracies, coupled two-contact iteration/next-frame cache, and nonfinite-input rejection. Run strict compilation and execution, then run a sanitizer build. Expected output is persistent-contact witness: 6 suites PASS. This verifies only the tested cases on the compiling environment; the repository GitHub Actions workflow repeats strict and undefined-behavior checks, with remote status to be verified separately. A reconstruction exercise is to add two bodies with unequal masses and an off-centre contact, compute kn by hand and compare every intermediate u_n, Δλ_n, Δv and Δω. A stronger follow-up exercise is to implement real feature matching, deliberately reverse normals between frames, and demonstrate that incorrectly reused cached tangential impulses generate artificial energy. Neither extension is presently claimed as implemented. Verified boundary and research questions The lab does not verify Kairo’s current renderer or physics engine, broadphase pair generation, narrowphase contact topology, 3D Jacobians, static/dynamic island management, precise multi-contact complementarity, numerical convergence across arbitrary scenes, determinism across compilers, robust CCD, or real-time performance. Before a research claim about stability or speed, define independent scene families, error metrics (maximum penetration, residual closing speed, drift, energy increase), iteration budgets, timestep families and order-randomization trials. Compare warm versus cold starts without changing geometry, feature matching or tolerances at the same time.. Open Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division — Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints. An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length. Prerequisites
Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Used by
Linear affine and projective transformations
Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Ray-triangle intersection - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Position reconstruction from depth Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Recall and next depth Explain why perspective division is nonlinear and why clipping must precede casual division. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Dividing the first three components by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration Phase 11 camera development Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership and non-owning views Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism By-value copies use member semantics, not recursive deep cloning. Rule-Zero composition delegates ownership to members; raw owners must coordinate transfer and release. Copying a pointer/view/handle is not acquiring ownership. Copying span/string_view or capturing a view by value copies only a descriptor. An owning string capture supplies independent storage; a view or handle does not automatically pin a deferred resource. The inline C++ laboratory distinguishes NamedVector::to_array, which copies values into a new array, from ArrayVector::view, which aliases actual array elements without owning them. Neither span nor pointer extends backing lifetime. Ownership and RAII are introduced as next-depth connections, not yet a full exception-safety treatment. M010 makes the distinction operational: an owner is responsible for release; a borrow only accesses. std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr retains a shared lifetime, and std::weak_ptr observes without extending that lifetime. Smart pointers do not remove the borrow/invalidation rules of raw pointers obtained from them. See RAII and resource handles and Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership. An owner controls a resource’s validity and release; a view merely refers to it. Vector owns its element buffer; span does not copy or prolong that buffer’s life. Owner destruction or invalidating reallocation can dangle the span. A reader retaining a span needs stable live backing for every read, not only at construction. Prerequisites
Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid. Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.
Used by
Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Deferred captures and borrowed views Copy semantics and resource identity Rules of Three Five and Zero RAII and resource handles Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership
Recall and next depth Explain why returning a view into a local vector fails. Pending: smart owners, shared immutable data and scheduling/resource pinning. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Directional and total derivatives — Directional and total derivatives Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism A directional derivative measures first-order change along a chosen direction. For a differentiable scalar field, it is the gradient paired with that direction; for a vector map, the Jacobian acts on the direction. The total derivative accounts for every input coordinate changing according to a path, combining partial derivatives with the rates of the coordinates themselves. A direction need not be normalized: normalization changes whether the derivative is per unit distance or per unit parameter. This distinction matters in signed-distance queries, motion paths, and parameterized camera projections. The total derivative clarifies the chain rule: if a state depends on time and an output depends on that state, the time rate is the local derivative composed with the state velocity. These are local statements, not global linearity claims. Prerequisites
Partial derivatives and gradients Derivative as a local linear map
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Atomic publication and durability — Atomic publication and durability Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Publishing a prepared temporary file by replacement concerns observers of the filesystem namespace. Crash durability concerns whether contents and namespace updates survive failures; it needs a specified platform/filesystem protocol. Neither follows from building a vector of bytes. The supplied AtomicFile excerpt is an unverified repository claim, not a tested durability guarantee. Prerequisites
Serialization — Publication persists already-specified bytes, rather than defining their format. Ownership and non-owning views — A mapping or publication pipeline must keep referenced bytes valid.
Used by Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept. Recall and next depth Name the observers and failure model for an atomic guarantee. Pending: Platform replacement semantics, flush ordering, recovery and cross-volume limits. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Executed POSIX durability sequence The durability contract now has an actual syscall-level witness in tools/labs/atomic_publication_durability_lab.cpp. The reference creates a staging file with exclusive creation, writes the complete payload, calls fsync on the file, closes it, renames it within the same directory, opens the containing directory, and calls fsync on that directory before treating publication as complete. It then verifies the final bytes and absence of the staging name. Separate tests reject a pre-existing staging file and a traversal-style final name. This is stronger than “write temp then rename,” because rename atomicity and durable persistence are different properties. The file sync requests persistence of file contents/metadata; the directory sync requests persistence of the directory-entry change. Successful calls on CI are evidence that the operating-system/filesystem accepted that ordering. They are not a laboratory power-cut test and cannot promise identical persistence guarantees on every filesystem, storage controller, Windows API, network filesystem or production asset pipeline.. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Object identity and generation handles — Object identity and generation handles Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism Copied handles are distinct C++ objects with equal application identities. A validated handle does not certify a previous component borrow; assignment may preserve a C++ slot while changing logical ownership. Object value, identity and address answer different questions. Equal values can belong to different objects; the same address can host successive lifetimes. A logical index/generation handle must be checked against the owning registry’s bounds, occupancy and generation. Counter wrap and registry identity remain policy obligations. Prerequisites
Object construction and storage reuse — Storage reuse creates successive occupants, motivating handles that record the intended generation.
Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Prefix scan and stream compaction — Prefix scan and stream compaction A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math> If each element says how many output records it will emit, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> is the first output slot owned by element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math>. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions. For Boolean compaction, let predicate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Scan <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> to obtain offsets. Every active element with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1]. Parallel structure The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> depth. On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:
scan each workgroup block into local output; record each block total; scan the block totals; add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.
Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct. Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup. Stream compaction as an allocation proof Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues. The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur. Evidence boundary The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing. Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.” Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions. Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.. Open Prefix scan and stream compaction in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Incremental contact penetration refresh — Incremental contact penetration refresh Position correction moves every contact point attached to the corrected bodies. For a small rotation, its first-order point displacement is translation plus rotation vector crossed with the pre-correction world-space lever arm. Project the difference of the two point movements onto the frozen contact normal, using the declared normal and penetration signs. Refresh each known contact once for the correction just applied, then reconsider the worst penetration. Reusing an old correction counts movement twice. This local estimate cannot discover new contacts or replace geometry refresh after substantial rotation or a feature change. Prerequisites
Concepts/Cross products and oriented area Concepts/Unit directions and safe normalization

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Interface contracts and publication — Interface contracts and publication An interface contract says more than which function name to call. It defines the states in which an operation is valid and what becomes true when it succeeds. A complete contract should state:
valid input domain and units; ownership and lifetime of arguments/results; mutation and aliasing; failure representation and exception/error guarantees; thread/concurrency rules; timing: immediate, deferred or asynchronous; invalidation; observability/publication point.
Publication is a state transition A producer may construct a resource privately and then publish it so consumers can rely on it. Before publication, partial state can remain invisible. After publication, every documented invariant must hold. For CPU concurrency, release/acquire synchronization is one possible publication mechanism when the memory model requirements fit the data structure. For asynchronous assets, “decode finished” does not mean “GPU resource is safe to sample.” A useful state machine may distinguish: requested → decoded → upload recorded → submitted → GPU-ready → published. Similarly, an obsolete request must not publish after a newer generation has replaced it. Generation IDs or request tokens protect the destination identity. Ownership versus readiness A reference can be alive but not ready. A GPU buffer wrapper can exist while its upload is still in flight. Conversely, a resource can be GPU-ready while the CPU owner is about to destroy it unless retirement is deferred until all GPU use completes. Lifetime and synchronization are independent axes. Failure guarantees If publication is atomic, consumers should observe either the old valid version or the new valid version, not a half-updated mixture. That promise requires implementation evidence appropriate to the domain: atomics/locks for CPU state, transaction/staging for files, semaphore/fence/queue dependencies for GPU work. Evidence tools/labs/threaded_asset_publication_lab.cpp and tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp exercise two different publication domains: concurrent asset decoding/publication and deterministic staged production publication. Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#An API is a promise about an operation. Related: Atomic publication and durability, Production manifests and transactional publication, Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.. Open Interface contracts and publication in Volume 1
